utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Re-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Colonel, you have before you this report of the sector for operations and staff affairs that we've been looking at, and it says members of the MUP conducted an operation against Siptar terrorists. Can we see from the report who conducted the operation? Is there any question here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no question here. It is evident that this action of the MUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We went through that yesterday. Don't go over matters that you have already dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not continue with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I was unable to find this in the meantime, but a page was also shown here from the daily report of the commander of this combat group 243/1 that was in Dulje and in Stimlje, and in this daily report, regular daily report, it was written: "No changes in the deployment of the unit for that day," the 15th. Does it mean that it was engaged or not engaged?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not engaged. That's what no changes means. No losses, no movement; status unchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the question regarding Walker, please tell us precisely, what was it that Walker told Loncar at this first meeting when they met? That was their first meeting. Where did it take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... precisely what it was that Walker said to Loncar. He wasn't there. We've gone through that exercise already. We've looked at -- we can look at what Loncar says in his statement, and is the matter relevant in any event?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you at that meeting, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation. I just didn't hear any interpretation. I can't hear anything from the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well -- are you now hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can now hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness was not at that meeting. How will he be in a position to say what Loncar said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't ask what Loncar said. I asked what Walker said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What Walker said. I mean, how will he be in a position to answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood, Mr. Robinson -- of course he cannot answer if he did not attend the meeting, but I understood that he did attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, did you attend that first meeting of Loncar and Walker?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday or the day before yesterday, I said that there was General Loncar, Mr. Walker, Colonel Mijatovic from the MUP of Kosovo and Metohija, and a lady interpreter named Gordana from the outpost of the Foreign Ministry in Pristina, and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's in the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That meeting he's talking about, as opposed to that meeting between Loncar and the accused, I don't think I asked him any questions about that meeting, and this really is about as tangential an issue as you can have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You asked the questions about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think about that meeting. I asked about the meeting with Milosevic, the accused. Because what was being suggested was how -- I'm reluctant to take time. It's being suggested that Walker asked to have Loncar there as opposed to Loncar being volunteered by the accused, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm going to allow the question on the basis that it can be said that it arises if only tangentially. So let us move on, Mr. Milosevic. Did you get an answer to the question that you asked?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted to hear what Walker had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the first meeting between Walker and Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Loncar -- in fact, Walker also met the chief of our outpost, Slana, on the -- at the official meeting for the first time 15th or 16th November, although he may have met with him unofficially earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Walker say on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Walker said to Loncar that he apologised to him for taking him away from the carefree leisure he had in his retirement, the walks with his grandson, et cetera. Because he had previously talked to you in Belgrade, he asked Dr. Loncar because they had had good cooperation in Slavonia and he remembered him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We are not going to dwell on that any longer. As for Walker's objectivity, could you please put on the ELMO just the first page and the last of page this Alliance for New Kosovo website paper. It says: "Kosovo should be an independent state in the full sense of the word." So that is this alliance. Let us see the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what this is said to relate to. I see how it's been introduced. Walker's objectivity. I didn't ask any questions about that. So I'd like to know where we're going.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the thrust of my questioning will become quite clear. I can't see it on the ELMO, though. Right. That's it. Could you please show the upper part so we can see the heading. Yes. Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, don't ask the question yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page now? Could you please show the last page now. It says: "Ambassador William Walker, former Special Representative of the UN in Eastern Slavonia ... and leader of the Kosovo Verification Mission." And then it goes on to enumerate members of this board of directors of that association. This relates to the questions that you answered concerning the objectivity and honesty of William Walker. Is he --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't remember asking any such questions. If I did, I did but I can't remember asking them. In any event, how does this arise? This is simply an effort to get in something that the accused believes may be unfavourable to Walker or may present Ambassador Walker in an unfavourable light to the audience he's playing to, and it's wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How does it arise, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this time Mr. Nice is trying to prove that the Verification Mission acted without bias and objectively, which is completely untrue. This is one of the proofs what that mission was like, and he has his hands in blood up to -- his arms in blood up to his shoulders, all the way back from Salvador.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will not allow the question, Mr. Milosevic. Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, would Your Honours look at the last sentence, and I invite the Chamber to discipline this accused. This is not a place for this accused to vent that type of observation from whatever emotions drive him against somebody who isn't here to answer them. It is quite improper. And frankly, if he can't behave properly, he should not be allowed to conduct his defence. I'm not here to defend witnesses, but it is absolutely outrageous that this court can be used for that sort of observation about a person who has been here as a witness and who is a man of international reputation. I say nothing more about it than that. Absolutely outrageous, and it should be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What statement are you referring to? I'm trying to see the statement to which you're referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to repeat it. It begins, "This is one of the proofs ..." What is said about this man is quite unacceptable and shouldn't be allowed in any court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must be careful in the comments that you make, the way you put questions concerning the character of witnesses, unless you have evidence to support what it is that you are putting. Do you have any other questions for this re-examination, bearing in mind the scope, the limits, and the purpose of re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. I always bear it in mind. My re-examination is extremely short, Mr. Robinson. Just a few more questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, you received here a statement of one soldier who was not named, and I am not going to name him myself, nor am I going to quote the statement. But Mr. Nice questioned you about some sort of activity that was aimed at directing Albanian civilians towards Korenica where allegedly men from the MUP were waiting for them with lists of terrorists, and then that area was cleansed, as was said here, from Albanians. And you, in your answer, said that it was not at all the objective of that operation. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the objective of that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of that operation was for the area of Reka which, according to our estimates, had --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not Reka. It's an area facing Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That entire area from Junik to Djakovica is called Reka. The objective was only to crush the terrorist forces in that area. We assessed that there was a brigade in that area about a hundred men strong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In one item in paragraph 42 in his statement - let me see - he said, as it says, "After civilians left, we set the houses on fire [In English] as this was the order." [Interpretation] Now, please, was there any order at any level issued on the part of the offices of the army of Yugoslavia, that is to say from the platoon commander, the lowest-level unit, not to go through all the units up to the top of the chain, to set any house intentionally on fire, and I stress intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we in the army had and have very capable officers, less capable officers, and incapable officers, but we didn't have any who were mentally deranged, and an order like that could have been issued only by someone who was mentally deranged, and I have no knowledge of anybody being like that in the army of Yugoslavia, any deranged officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in paragraph 44 he goes on to say that a soldier from our battalion, he says, was killed. Was it possible that civilians killed this soldier from his battalion in his battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that the unit did suffer one casualty. There was one death. I knew that Vukovic -- with Vukovic there were several wounded persons and one killed person. So they did suffer casualties during the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in paragraph 45, and I don't want to mention names, to name names, I don't wish to say that I have identified witnesses in this way, but anyway, he was a captain, ordered the four Albanian hostages "to carry [In English] the body of our killed soldier," [Interpretation] and so on and so forth. Now, I'm interested in this word "hostages." Did the unit of the Yugoslav army take hostages at all at any time during any kind of action or operation against the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I hear of anything like that, that somebody took hostages when it comes to the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, fine. Thank you, Colonel. And just a few more questions for you now. At the beginning, Mr. Nice -- that is to say at the beginning of the cross-examination, Mr. Nice asked you what you were doing at that time, during the material time. Now, throughout the time you performed your work as head of the team of the Pristina Corps for liaising with the Verification Mission. Throughout that time did you retain your post and position as chief of the service of the artillery in the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Infantry -- sorry, infantry; interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have your liaising job to do with the team?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the officers in the battalions conducted their regular affairs and also their job as liaison officer. At the time, I had three functions to perform. I was the head of the team for liaising with the Verification Mission on behalf of the Pristina Corps. I was Mr. Loncar's assistant in the federal commission for relations with the Verification Mission, and I was chief of the artillery service in the infantry service until the 10th of March. Until the 10th of March, I was just a member of the team for the Verification Mission. After that, I continued to be chief of infantry, and I was no longer Loncar's assistant because General Brankovic arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Nice said you were replaced from your duty, which is something that Ciaglinski claimed in his statement. You said that it wasn't that you were replaced but that there was a reshuffling. Were you in fact replaced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned a diagram or schematic of the organisation that we saw at the beginning of the General Staff, then the team of the General Staff, the team of the 3rd Army, the team of the Pristina Corps. We saw all that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no longer the Pristina Corps team. There was just one unified team of the army and the Pristina Corps. They provided one team, one single team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, up to the 10th of March, what did General Brankovic do? What was his function?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brankovic came from Belgrade on the 10th with a team of the 26 verifiers, the new ones who came with a knowledge of the English language to replace the liaison officers in all the garrisons and in all the border battalions, and people from the army of Yugoslavia came who knew English, who could speak English. And Brankovic was among them. He came with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with that reshuffling and reorganisation, was the army team joined up with the corps team so that instead of having two teams you had one team?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. Two merged to create one. From the army and Pristina Corps one team was set up. Until the reorganisation was put in place, led -- at the head of the army team, we had General Mladenovic, and his deputy was Selovic [phoen]. And you can see that from all the signatures up until the 10th. From the 10th onwards you only see the signature of Colonel Petrovic who was at the head of that joint team. And you can see that by the signatures. It was no longer the old army Pristina team. It was reorganised to form a single team with the changes that were put in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After about a week after the reorganisation, the mission precipitously withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th in the early morning hours it set off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These 26 officers who knew English and the general reshuffling and enlargement of the team and making the organisation simpler by abolishing the different levels in the team, would anybody have done that for just a space of some seven days or was that in fact done under the assumption that the cooperation would be long-lasting, or longer lasting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody would conduct a reorganisation of that kind, bring in so many officers, train them in their job if they thought it was going to last so long. At a lecture given by General DZ which was held with the goal of cooperation, what he expected, the problems he encountered and so on, so he held a lecture to those officers in the army club of the 15th Brigade where that course was taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Ciaglinski, in the statement shown to you by Mr. Nice, says that the team came to upset relations with the mission. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very silly. I told him that a team would come in to improve the work of the team, because they knew the language, and that was their sole undertaking and job, because the officers had other business to attend to. And I think in my notebook it says that on two occasions we discussed this matter and they said that there were problems with liaison officers in more subordinate units, and there's a document by the corps commander. So this was a necessity and was taken up in several of the reports where it says that one united team should be created from the army team and Pristina team and that other officers should be brought in, and that was indeed done. In the space of one month the officers were trained and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in any way whatsoever could we explain matters as Ciaglinski explained it, because he says that you were replaced to have better relations with the mission.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's a complete lie, completely incorrect, and he said many other things like that too, along those lines. I don't want to comment on them now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the questions that had to do with how you were able to establish that he testified, was it in public session that everything was stated except the name when Ciaglinski testified?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A high-ranking officer from the command said and drew on the map. I personally followed that part of the proceedings, and everybody could deduce who it was because you knew who he -- we knew who he contacted, who he was in contact with. He was in daily contact with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's all I wanted to clarify. Now, Mr. Nice also asked you what you were doing. You said a moment ago that you were a chief of the infantry service in the corps, and by virtue of that function, you were a member of the corps, were you not, by the same token?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that unusual? Because in your career you were a brigade commander --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for six years I was a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after the brigade commander, you went to the staff corps and were head of the infantry service which made up 80 per cent of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, 60 per cent of the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, 60 per cent of the corps. Now, is it usual that a corps commander sends one of his assistants, a member of the staff, out into the terrain on the ground to somebody in the corps to check out and verify the situation, to carry out an inspection, to establish the difficulties they were encountering, and to report back? Was that customary or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is the chief of a service, that he should do this, and that was a motorised company, and I was head of the 125th Brigade at Kosare at one time. And after the breakthrough at Kosare, I was sent there urgently to assess the situation and help the brigade command in solving its problems, and that's what we did throughout that time; that was our basic task.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down for the benefit of the interpreters and the Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and the witness, the interpreter is asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Commenting on questions related to Racak, Mr. Nice said that the action was launched against the village. Now, I'm asking you as a professional soldier, as a professional man, if the police enters a village in search of terrorists, is the action being waged against the village? Can that be qualified in that way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, you can't use an expression like that. It's completely distorted. Just like it's not a whole nation that is to blame for something, so also you don't carry out an action against a whole village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You dwelt during the cross-examination on tab 14 for some time, and Mr. Nice also showed you something from some sort of blue book, a report on events which were described in a document of yours found in tab 14. Now, could you explain just briefly, please, Colonel, in that tab, tab 14, as far as I was able to follow, it was the -- the minutes of a meeting and said that Drewienkiewicz personally checked out the information.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He established that they were not correct, and as far as I remember having heard, but you can read it out here, he said that was normal, legitimate activity. That's how he qualified it, and that's what was recorded in those minutes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Let me just take a moment to find it. This is what he said. I'll read it out to you slowly. I heard last time or, rather, I was told that I was speaking too fast last time. Ciaglinski said that General DZ was in Kacanik and Ivaja, and that he established that there had been conflicts, that there was firing, that certain houses were damaged but that there was no plundering. Instead, certain houses from which members of the KLA had fired were searched, which they considered to be a normal procedure. Therefore, the situation is not even remotely such as described by some media and the KLA, with the latter claiming that villages had been destroyed, burnt, et cetera. He added that we had a witness on the ground who would refute the KLA allegations in his report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain to us now, please, how come he informed you of this and of these minutes of that date, that he would deny the allegations, refute them, and then in the blue book which was shown to you by Mr. Nice it says what Drewienkiewicz in fact established was not true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd just like to say that these minutes were kept by Mr. Soskic from the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs, their sector, and you had all the people there who were in embassies. He was a very reliable man. He knew English well. Slana, as the head of that sector, signed the document of that field office, and there was no reason why our document from our conversation should be falsified or something else written other than had actually taken place at the meeting. Now, when the blue book is mentioned here, I'd just like to say what I already said once before, that I doubted the sincerity of the reporting and the veracity of the reporting. When you asked me whether it was proper reporting or not I said that I doubted that it was. With respect to what Mr. Nice showed me in the blue book and what happened here tells us in fact that things were written up differently. I know that they had one team who did not allow the verifiers to check out matters on the ground. And there were even cases where some people didn't wish to sign a record that was compiled and that was placed as an exhibit here. There are documents about the explosion of a mine near Morina. They came to conduct an on-site investigation. They said that it was a serious border incident. But when it came to signing the minutes and record, they didn't want to say that we're going to send it to Pristina, you'll be informed. Now, in Pristina, within the frameworks of the Verification Mission, they had the body where they collected all the information, and then they would grade the information that came in and decide what was what, what was more important and what was less important. But as I say, they didn't trust all the verifiers because they didn't have enough experience to be able to verify the situation on the ground. So if DZ, if General DZ was not able to verify something on the spot as a general, then I don't know how the team could have done that either, and who was best placed to determine what was what, whereas these minutes cannot be taken as having been written like that, as Mr. Nice suggested, just for ourselves. We inform our -- this is to inform our own organs. So we can't disinform them. That wasn't our goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have something in relation to what Mr. Nice asked you which had to do with the statement made by Ciaglinski, who said the following -- we're not going to go into matters we've already cleared up but he said you gave him or you provided him with maps of the positions which NATO used later on.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a complete lie. Mr. Ciaglinski asked, and I think he was there with an Irish brigadier general at the time when he came to see me, if I remember correctly. I'm not quite sure but he did come several times with a brigadier general from Ireland to attend the meeting with Ciaglinski and myself, and I think that I might have given him those maps in his presence. They asked for the maps to have different sources of information. They had certain maps, we had certain maps, so there was some discrepancy between those maps, and the scale was 1:100.000, as I've said, without the deployment of units, and I think that Ciaglinski showed the map. If the map is in existence, I would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I understood you correctly, you provided them with these maps to avoid any misunderstanding because of the discrepancy in the maps, the different maps that the Verification Mission had and the maps that we had.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the basic reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's what you did, with the knowledge of your superior officers, without any - how shall I put this? - without any other complications that this would involve.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no complications or impediments at all. I was a member of the staff team in the corps, and I informed them of all the events, and they would receive written reports every day. So everybody knew about that. It wasn't anything underhand. I had to receive the maps first, and once I had received the maps myself, then I handed them on. And we have to be issued maps, and when we're issued maps, we have to say why we need them; whether for training, for a war plan, or whatever. You can't just take maps without giving a reason for why you need them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite understandable, of course. So thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that concludes my re-examination, as you see, Mr. Robinson, in the briefest possible time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel Kotur, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I explain my position -- I beg Your Honour's pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The notebook may be returned to the witness. It has been copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. When the witness has withdrawn I will make one observation about that and one observation, with your leave, in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, overnight we've looked again at the text of that book, and this morning another look at the book itself. I certainly don't seek it to become an exhibit. Something deeply unsatisfactory about this sort of material which was rather trailed for us to ask to see by an observation of the accused. I accept nothing about that document. I don't accept that it's genuine or contemporaneous, and it -- the whole circumstances of its production make it increasingly important that we should have access to, wherever possible with these witnesses, contemporaneous documents provided pursuant to our RFAs in advance. There would have been questions to ask about -- some questions to ask about the content of the book, but it would have taken far too long, and it didn't seem to us therefore worth seeking to have it made an exhibit. May I invite the Chamber to give me one minute in private session for a reason that I think will be justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before that, could you tell us the reason why you believe that notebook is not a contemporaneous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are several reasons why I'm not prepared to accept that it's contemporaneous. Just looking at the notebook itself, the way it's been written, its pristine condition, the inks, the selected dates. All sorts of reasons that simply cast serious doubt in the mind of an inquiring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that does not necessarily mean that the witness made up the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't say. His answers about the notebook were also extraordinary, in my -- in our submission, saying he didn't make notebooks, he did make notebooks, somehow he had this one which was an official notebook but it hadn't been registered to him and that's the reason he kept it. But if you look at the notebook itself -- I mean, he's still here, you can have a look at it, but I'm not inviting you to do so -- there is not continuity of dates, the writing appears all to have been done at a piece, but that's not a matter for me really to say. There are all sorts of reasons why this is not a document one would let in without careful examination if it was central to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it is regrettable that you are making these comments about the witness and the notebook when you did not seek to put those questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was no time. This document was produced at the last minute. And this is exactly the problem that the accused is creating for us. If he wishes to rely on contemporaneous documents -- and you see, he trailed the problem for us by saying -- I have it here. There's -- it's in your materials. You have a document. We reached exactly this sort of problem. Now, here's a man who -- forget this man. All these witnesses that we've been hearing from are witnesses who made contemporaneous documents that should have been provided either under RFAs or in advance of their giving evidence, and it is the Court that is being inconvenienced in the extreme by having to deal with these issues at the last minute or, alternatively, simply not dealing with them because I decline to do so because I can't do so in the time available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I doubt if you would have tolerated these remarks from the accused, because what you've done is say, well, we'll not exhibit this - so that means it's not before the Trial Chamber - but nevertheless here is why, and by implication, inviting us to reflect these submissions in our assessment of the witness. And I want to make it clear here and now that these comments will not, as presently advised because they have no status, form any part of my assessment of this witness. The situation may, of course, change between now and that stage, but I think it right to make that clear at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy with that. I explained my position and I don't wish it to form any part of the evidence or consideration one way or another. But the general point remains that this type of document, when it's produced to us in the way it is being produced, creates this generic type of problem, and the Court knows that it is being toyed with by the authorities - forget this witness - in non-production of documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know that, Mr. Nice, and that is another regrettable comment. You are a senior Prosecutor and a professional, and you have to be as careful with the comments that you make as the accused has to be too. That's irresponsible. The Court does not know that it is being toyed with by the authorities. That is not the position of this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And may I say two things. I recognise the general point - I think it's the one valid point you're making - that there does appear to be difficulty in getting hands-on contemporaneous material. That's a perfectly valid comment. But the second point is this: You know now that there is to be a hearing in relation to attempts to recover certain material. You know, therefore, that there is to be a forum very shortly for you to make appropriate comments along the lines that you've now embarked upon when it will be appropriate for all parties who need to to make comments. So this is not the time, I would suggest, for that sort of assertion to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honours please. And I will indeed make good my observations at that hearing. I know there is a hearing. I don't yet know the detail of its purpose. I know about it in only the most general terms. And I'll end this, if I may, with a repetition and emphasis of the fact that the accused must know that this Chamber will be assisted by advance production of contemporaneous documents to which witnesses can speak and that this Court is inconvenienced in the extreme by not having that material to hand. Your Honours, may we go into private session for the other matter, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Are we in public session now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to the objections raised by Mr. Nice concerning the notebook of Colonel Kotur, I assume that you are aware of the fact, like I am, that he expressed some rather grave doubts, inter alia that all of it was written at the same time, that it's not authentic, and so on, not genuine. And he also said that it was in pristine condition. I have had books for decades that are in pristine condition. This can only testify to the fact that Colonel Kotur is a tidy person. But please, experts can have a look at this. He mentioned ink and whatever. They can say, the experts, whether this is contemporaneous or not. That's quite easy. Another thing I wanted to say. I also did not know that he had this notebook. I wish to remind you of the fact that in response to some question he quite simply said that he remembered that because he had it written down in his notebook, and that's how it happened in the first place that this notebook was brought up. There was no intention of using that notebook for the simple reason that I had not know about it. Had he told me during the proofing, "I have a notebook," I would have read it, or Professor Rakic would have read it, or one of my associates would have read it. So it cropped up spontaneously. Colonel Kotur had it on him and in your own presence you saw how this notebook appeared. I would not accept that, voicing suspicions of this kind vis-a-vis a high-ranking officer of the Yugoslav army concerning a notebook that he mentioned with good intentions and even proffered here when asked for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. The Chamber commented on the remarks by the Prosecutor. In fact, reprimanded him for those remarks. They're not part of the evidence. And I take note of your observation that some people are better custodians of their books than others. Your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just raise an administrative matter before the next witness? It's not going to take up more than a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, could you please make a decision regarding my medical treatment at the institute in Moscow? I would like to note that since August I have had difficulties, and that was established at the Leiden University as well by Dr. Dalal, and this bothers me a great deal. Experts at the Moscow institute think that they have -- that these problems are of a vascular origin, and they think they can help. I believe that this kind of medical treatment is indispensable for me, so could you kindly rule on it. That's all I had to say, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber recently received the last piece of information necessary for it to give full consideration to this matter, and we'll be giving a decision shortly. Your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness is Professor Dr. Branko Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Kostic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state the briefest possible information about yourself. Where were you born? Where did you live? Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 28th of August, 1939 in Rvasi, near Rijeka Crnojevica, municipality of Cetinje in Montenegro. I completed elementary school in Rvasi, my native village, and I continued schooling while staying in boarding schools or orphanages, because my father was executed by Italian fascists in 1942. So I spent my childhood years in orphanages. Zagreb, Herceg-Novi and Kotor are the towns where I went to school, and I completed my secondary education in Titograd, now Podgorica. I graduated from the University of Belgrade school of economics, and that's the same university where I got my master's degree and ultimately my Ph.D. Practically, after I finished university and after finishing my military service, which I did at the school of reserve officers in Zadar at the artillery school, and after doing my internship in Niksic, after that I started living in Podgorica, Montenegro, and that's where I live to the present day. I'm married. My wife is also a Ph.D. -- also has a Ph.D. in economics, and she is a member of the Academy of Sciences and Arts too of Montenegro. We have two daughters. The older daughter has doctorate in electrotechnical studies and she works as an electrical engineering researcher, and my younger daughter has a doctorate in law, international private law, and she works as a senior lecturer at the University of Montenegro in Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us briefly what your career was, what positions you held, and briefly about your political career as well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: My first professional position was a political position at the same time, and that was the organisation secretary of the University Committee of the League of Communists of the University of Belgrade. I spent a year and a half in that position as a university student. It was a professional job, though, so practically, once I graduated, I came back to Podgorica, to Titograd, with a year and a half of service. After that for five years I worked as a professional president of the youth organisation of Montenegro, and then at my own request, because I did not want to get too far away from my professional line of work, I started working at the aluminum combine which was being founded at that time, and I was commercial manager and general manager there for ten years. After that, I started working at the University of Montenegro, the technical faculties there, and for eight years I worked at the Institute for Technical Research there, and at the same time I taught the students of all technical faculties. I actually lectured them on political economy. That is part of the general curriculum at technical faculties. And practically until my retirement last year or, rather, the year before last I was retired as a full professor. And in the meantime, I had a few political positions as well. From 1986 until 1989, I was vice-president of the Executive Council of Montenegro in the government of Mr. Vuk Vukadinovic. After that, I was president of the Presidency of Montenegro for two years. After being relieved of that duty, I was for a few months president of the delegation of Montenegro in the Chamber of Republics and Provinces of the Federal Assembly of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And after that, I was elected to the Presidency of the SFRY, and a month and a half later I became vice-president of the Presidency of the SFRY. After having held that office, around the 15th of June, 1992, I withdrew from political life. I returned to the University of Montenegro, and that's where I ended my career.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me briefly what the position of the Presidency of Montenegro was when you were in that position.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The president -- I was president of the Presidency of Montenegro in the period from 1989 until 1990. According to the constitution of Montenegro, this was a collective organ in the republic. In addition to myself, there were four other members of the Presidency, and it can be said that, according to the constitution, this was largely a ceremonial post because it was the government that actually was in charge of conducting domestic and foreign policies. But it was a highly representative function. In the hierarchy, it was the top position, the top office in the Republic of Montenegro, and we received regular information, not only about what was going on in Montenegro but what was going on in the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. 1989 and 1990; right? So you received regular information about what went on in Yugoslavia, throughout Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that how I can understand what you've just said now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, after 1990, you were president of the delegation of Montenegro in the Chamber of Republics and Provinces in the Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, as for that office, like in any country, it is the parliament and the legislation, therefore, of the country. But as president of the delegation of Montenegro in that Assembly, of course we followed all developments which already then became rather dramatic. And we received information, perhaps not in such great detail like when I was president of the Presidency. There were some bulletins that were issued by the Secretariat of the Interior of the republic, but also the federal secretariat, of the interior, that is. So these were the bulletins involved. We also had bulletins containing information from our foreign service, the diplomatic service, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about confidential information here.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also everyday life. While you were president of the Presidency of Montenegro, as for this confidential information coming from the foreign service and coming from the interior, did you have knowledge about everything that happened in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, because as that kind of officeholder, I had consultations, meetings, talks, in addition to the regular type of information that any citizen receives from the media. We followed the work of the government, of the republic, and of the federal government too, so we were kept abreast of developments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for Montenegro, what was your position and what were your views?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: When the change of government took place, when all of this happened, and often they were referred to in our part of the world as the happening of the people. I was Prime Minister at the time, so with all this turbulence and these mass rallies, no one asked the government of Montenegro to resign, but nevertheless we as the government were the first to resign. Not because somebody had asked us to do that but because we thought that since resignations were sought at these mass rallies from the holders of top political positions in the federation of Yugoslavia, we thought that we as the government should submit our resignation straight away and in this way we could lead to an alleviation of the situation, to the cooling of passions, because not everybody was asked to resign. However, we thought that in this way it would be easier for the others to resign, too, whose resignations were really being asked for. It was a rather dramatic time in Titograd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the reasons of this mass dissatisfaction of the citizens as far as the policy of the up-to-then-leadership of Montenegro was concerned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: An explanation of this would probably require a lengthy answer, but I'll try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: As brief as possible. There were several reasons. In my assessment, and perhaps that is due to the fact that, well, I'm a professional economist, I'm convinced that one of the main reasons for the fact that it happened precisely at that time is of an economic nature. I'm talking about now I experienced this in Montenegro. The entire economy of Montenegro was in a high state of crisis at that time. It was about to collapse. And not only the Presidency of Montenegro that I was elected to later but also the previous Presidency of Montenegro, which was chaired by academician Dr. Bozin Ivanovic [phoen] at the time, and also the government of Montenegro, the previous one and the new one, kept going back to this very bad economic situation in Montenegro. And how should I put this? We were always really furious with the federal government and Mr. Ante Markovic as we were sure that he started dealing with political matters more and the establishment of his own political party rather than as federal Prime Minister, deal with economic matters and make it possible to have a better economic situation in Montenegro. Let me just give an example of what was going on in the economic field. Montenegro was an underdeveloped area, and as some other underdeveloped areas in Montenegro, from the fund for the accelerated development of the underdeveloped areas of Yugoslavia, it received aid. This was the time of one-party system, so the Presidency and the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and the Presidency of Yugoslavia as a state organ and as the government believed that Montenegro, in spite of that aid, was lacking behind in its development and it required additional resources. Therefore, in the desire to speed up the development of Montenegro, it was made possible for Montenegro to borrow abroad, and Montenegro did get additional borrowing from abroad. At that time our currency was not convertible, as it is today. We had dinars, Yugoslav dinars, and these foreign currency loans were obtained by Montenegro not in foreign currency but in dinars from the national bank of Yugoslavia. However, the foreign currency that was in the national bank was available to much better developed economies in Croatia and Slovenia, and they used them to develop their economic capacities. But when time came to pay back, Montenegro had to pay back in foreign currency. Due to the general economic situation, enterprises in Montenegro had to use all their resources to do that, because they had to use the dinars to buy the foreign currency from the national bank to pay back the loans. And a solution was found in the federal government to help Montenegro deal with foreign currency discrepancies, changes in foreign exchange rates. What happened, the federal government and Prime Minister Ante Markovic were almost a year late in paying to Montenegro these exchange rate differences and Montenegro had no choice but to take short-term loans on the market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To cut a long story short, the behaviour of the federal government put Montenegro in a very unenviable position economically.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was coming to that. Only for interest rates on the loans that Montenegro had to take due to this lateness of aid from the federal government, Montenegro had to take 300 billion dinars. In addition to these economic difficulties, we had other difficulties, but we -- when we put it all together, our people say that we were too greedy maybe. We wanted cake rather than bread. And this all resulted in these mass demonstrations, rallies. But not only that. There began certain displays of nationalism. And that dated back to a long time ago. We all know about the Croatian spring of 1971. And because of their participation in that nationalist movement, some people, including some who later became important officials, including Stipe Mesic, went to prison. In 1981 there were mass demonstrations of extremists and separatists in Kosovo. Later, especially after Tito's death in 1980, the situation in Kosovo deteriorated and the secessionist forces gained strength. Republics, and especially leaderships in Slovenia and Croatia, even back then evidently supported the separatist leadership in Kosovo, reckoning that if the situation gets tough over there, if there is an insurgency, that would make it easier for them to secede and become independent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I appreciate the need for this kind of information, but it's more helpful to proceed by way of question and answer rather than a long narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, you've just explained for the most part the reasons for popular discontent. They were mainly economic, but also political to some extent. Could we summarise it that way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the demands, popular demands at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in Montenegro there were a lot of our people, citizens of Montenegro, who both after the First and the Second World War populated one part of Kosovo and Metohija called Metohija. There were a lot of Montenegrin migrants in that area. And you have to know that Montenegro is very small and we all know each other. Those migrants in Kosovo left behind their families, extended families, relatives. And there was this decade-long pressure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pressure on whom?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: On Montenegrins in Kosovo who had to go back to Montenegro, and that created discontent among our people, because Montenegro viewed federal authorities as not active enough. And you have to know that after the First World War, Pec had the largest number of Montenegrins relative to the overall population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened later?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian leadership managed to obtain the agreement of the federal party leadership, the Central Committee, and so on, to adopt constitutional amendments, because until that time, Serbia was in an unequal position compared to others. It had two autonomous provinces, and the Assemblies of these provinces were able to adopt legislation without the approval of Serbia, whereas Serbia was unable to adopt any legislation without the approval of both provinces. And I think that a tug-of-war at the federal level lasted for two or three years, and finally Serbia managed to amend its constitution. And it's completely untrue to say that Serbia put an end to the autonomy of the provinces in that way. The leaderships in Kosovo and Metohija on one hand, and in Vojvodina on the other hand, had secessionist -- or, rather, autonomist leanings and only a popular movement could contribute to bringing about a change in these leaderships as well. What I was saying about the situation in Montenegro a moment ago means that it affected us as well. Our Montenegrin leadership was rather indifferent, or seemed rather indifferent to the fate of Montenegrins in Kosovo who had to leave, and their conduct caused a revolt. In August 1988 [Realtime transcript read in error "1998"] - and you have to know that the month of August is an extremely hot month in Montenegro, with temperatures going up to 40 or even 45 degrees Centigrade - there was a rally that was supposed to be organised in the afternoon when the heat is not so bad. It was scheduled for 4.00 p.m. The minister of the interior allowed that rally to happen but only at noon and the masses, the people understood this as a provocation, and that also caused more discontent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did these protest rallies end?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, the longer they lasted, the more people rallied, and the leadership, the party leadership included, were asked to resign. So the state leadership of Montenegro did submit their irrevocable resignations on the 10th of January, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you referred to a rally in the month of August in, according to the transcript, 1998. Did you actually say 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said 1998, but I corrected myself immediately and said 1988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. One other matter. You're talking about the resignation of the party leadership, and earlier when you were discussing that, you said at that time you were Prime Minister, but in the earlier summary you gave of your curriculum vitae, you made no reference to being Prime Minister. Is that another interpretation error or was there a point at which you were in fact Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President of the Executive Council. It must be an interpretation error, because I didn't state at any point this morning that I was Prime Minister. I said I was Deputy Prime Minister in the government of Prime Minister Vuk Vukadinovic. That's what I said verbatim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is it right that you described that position as vice-president of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will quote to you now from the 78th paragraph of the Kosovo indictment against me. "Starting with July 1988 until March 1989, a series of demonstrations and rallies supportive of Slobodan Milosevic's policies, the so-called anti-bureaucratic revolution, took place in Vojvodina and Montenegro. This protest led to the ouster of the respective provincial and republican governments. The new governments were then supportive of and indebted to Slobodan Milosevic." End of quote. Now, please, were the rallies of demonstrations and -- in Vojvodina and Montenegro supportive of Slobodan Milosevic, or did they have other objectives? Don't repeat what you've already said, just answer my question.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I could not testify so reliably to the situation in Vojvodina, but I have said already that even the leadership in Vojvodina, despite the constitutional changes to the constitution of Serbia, had separatist leanings and there was pressure on them to resign and to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is quite all right if you reply only to questions regarding Montenegro. I quoted a paragraph of the indictment, but if something does not apply to Montenegro, just skip it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: In relation to Montenegro, I could say the following: I would be less than honest if while describing that situation and those developments I failed to mention that your name at that time shone brightly on the political arena of the entire federal Yugoslavia. And in that atmosphere of indifference to many problems, you appeared as a relatively young person, a person whom I remembered from my party work. In my second year at the university, you were the party secretary at the university, but after that I lost sight of you. But seemingly overnight you appeared on the political arena of Serbia and Yugoslavia, and many people saw you as a person who would be finally able to make things move, to get things going. That was my impression. And in my first interview when I was elected president of the Presidency, the interview that I gave to a party newspaper called Borba, I said that a huge mass of people of various political beliefs rallied around these convictions and around that movement, probably with different expectations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't have to go so far abroad, but I quoted to you one particular passage. These new governments were then supportive of and indebted to Slobodan Milosevic. So I'm asking you as a direct participant in those events, is your knowledge consistent with the claim that somebody supported me or organised rallies of support to me and then became indebted to me over that support and, as my debtor, continued to support me? Is that consistent with what you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, it sounds like nonsense to me. If a government or a leadership were supportive of you, then it would be normal for you to feel indebted to them, not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just read it as an example of the kind of thing that you can find in this indictment. When did you become president of the Presidency of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The Assembly of Montenegro elected me in April of 1991, and the rotation in the Presidency happened regularly every 15th of May. However, my election, according to the constitution, had to be confirmed by both chambers of the Federal Assembly. They had not done so by the 15th of May. They did so on the 16th, so it is practically on the 16th of May I became president [as interpreted] of the Presidency of the SFRY, and on the 30th of June or the 1st of July, I became vice-president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were elected in May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: April, by the Assembly of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was their duty to nominate a member of the Presidency for Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: And the Presidency had to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on, it may be another transcript difficulty. The suggestion is that you became president of the Presidency on the 16th of May. I suspect you simply became a member of the Presidency on the 16th of May. Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be an interpretation error. I did not say that a moment ago. What I said was that the Federal Assembly of the SFRY confirmed my election by the Assembly of Montenegro on the 16th of May. It confirmed my election as member of the Presidency of the SFRY, and from that time on I was a member of the Presidency of the SFRY. However, since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only one word is wrong here in the transcript. When it says "member." Actually, it should read "member," and it reads "president," and that's the only thing. Can you answer this question: Why did there occur a crisis in the Presidency of the SFRY in mid-March 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I know that, because by that time I already handed over my duties of president [as interpreted] of Presidency of Montenegro to Momir Bulatovic, who was newly elected, but I was heading the delegation of Montenegro in the Federal Assembly, and our Yugoslav public opinion as well as the international public opinion were familiar with the problems and the famous or notorious session of the Presidency of the SFRY in March that lasted so long. The basic problem that occurred with that session when the work of the Presidency was paralysed was reflected in the fact that the top echelons of the Yugoslav People's Army, quite correctly, I believe, and quite appropriately, analysed the developments and assessed the oncoming events, and the military leadership then suggested to the Presidency of the SFRY, which was the Supreme Commander of armed forces, to introduce a state of emergency. And that's what paralysed the work of the Presidency, because four members were against imposing a state of emergency whereas the other four members were in favour, in favour of allowing the military leadership to forestall the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what should have been the contents and goal of the measures proposed, to prevent international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, in addition to the highly -- high degree of tension in Kosovo, and I have to say the very open support and biased support of the leading politicians from Slovenia and Croatia and their support to the separatists in Kosovo, the situation became increasingly tense, both on the territory of Slovenia and on the territory of Croatia itself. And at that time, there was a clandestine import of weapons going on which was used to arm the paramilitary formations. The weapons were being distributed even to civilians according to their party affiliations, and I said at the time that that was the first time after World War II that something like that was going on, that civilians were being issued weapons based on their party affiliation, and that was the characteristic of the Croatian democratic community, the HDZ, on the territory of Croatia. But once things had escaped control, there was more and more arming of civilians, not only in Croatia and by the HDZ but also in other parts of the country as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We left off discussing the crisis in the Presidency and the proposals by the staff of the Supreme Command. You explained that to us. Now, who were the groups that were illegally armed that the Supreme Command staff referred to at the time and who needed to be disarmed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, they were paramilitary formations in Croatia, paramilitary formations in Slovenia. That is to say the Slovenian leadership justified themselves by saying it wasn't a paramilitary unit, that they were there for the Territorial Defence, and it was the Territorial Defence that had been turned into their army, but they omitted from view of the fact that Territorial Defence, pursuant to the constitution of Yugoslavia, was a part and parcel of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, and by the same taken, everything we're discussing now took place in the first half of 1991 whereas in the indictment it states that Yugoslavia, the SFRY, existed until April 1992. Therefore, it was paramilitary formations that were armed, it was citizens who were armed, and quite simply they needed to be disarmed. Let me just tell you of a fact that was bandied about fairly often while I was in the SFRY Presidency to the effect that the Croatian police forces in just two months had grown from 17.000 policemen that they had in peacetime to over 90.000 in the space of just two months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did this illegal arming go on for of these irregular forces in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you an exact answer or say a period of time, but quite obviously it couldn't have been imported clandestinely all at once. I know the channels came in from Hungary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just going to ask you a few questions now to which I consider you could give just yes or no answers, perhaps, but of course you're the best judge of that and can give broader answers if necessary, but only if necessary, please. The authorities of Croatia, the authorities in Croatia, did they recognise the fact that there was illegal arming going on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what evidence and proof existed that such weapons were coming in?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all there were reports, intelligence reports from the intelligence services, both military and civilian of Yugoslavia, but the Croatian authorities would refute this time and again. However, the intelligence services, the KOS, the army intelligence service taped a secret film.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that. So you're saying that evidence and proof did exist. That will suffice for the moment. Now, did the Croatian authorities accept undertaking the disarmament of these irregular formations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The Croatian authorities accepted that these formations should be disarmed, if my information is correct, but I think that they agreed only once the film went public and was shown in public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, was this promise taken on as an obligation by the Croatian government? Was it fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No. The Presidency -- well, I wasn't in the Presidency myself at the time, but I did follow events. I think on the 9th of January, the SFRY Presidency took a decision to have all paramilitary formations disarmed on the territory of the whole country, and then this was followed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you say this Presidency decision came?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of January. Then on the 24th or 5th of January - I don't remember exactly - the military organs and military court in Zagreb and the judiciary there took into custody a certain number of participants in this clandestine importing of weapons, and also there was an arrest warrant put out for the arrest of General Spegelj. However, I seem to remember that the Croatian Defence Council rejected that accusation according to which he was thought to be the direct organiser of this clandestine import of weapons, so he was not arrested, he wasn't taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago a film that was taped, that was filmed by the Military Intelligence Service. Do you know anything about why the film showing Croatian clandestine arming was filmed in the first place and why it was shown?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I often asked myself that question, even when I took my place in the Presidency. To me, it would appear more normal had the services taken in the perpetrators, the actors in the film, and then having the film shown on television rather than the other way round, showing the film first and then trying to bring the perpetrators to justice. Because that film was so shocking, had a shocking effect on the Yugoslav public, and you can imagine how much fear it instilled in the population and how shocking it was to the Serb population living in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who gave permission for the film to be aired?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was the top echelons in the military but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we take a look at a brief excerpt, a brief clip from that footage? Professor Rakic was kind enough to assist the booths, the technical booths for showing these films -- this footage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The arming of the illegal HDZ army is going at full speed which is an indicator that a Croatian terrorist armada is being formed. Although the formal request for the arming of the HDZ army are being made at the competent institutions in the country, the Croatian leadership is setting into motion mechanisms for mass arming from foreign military warehouses. The president of the republic, Tudjman, and Minister Boljkovac had a number of contacts with arms producers in the world. Most understanding was shown by the Hungarians who opened their military warehouses wide. On the 11th of October already in 1990, the first shipment of arms arrived by Cazmatrans from Bjelovar. It crossed the Hungarian-Yugoslav border. From two storehouses of weapons in the vicinity of Budapest package was sent from an organisation Astra [phoen] from Zagreb, and it contained 450 packages containing 4.500 automatic rifles of the Kalashnikov type and the necessary quantity of ammunition. The Federal Secretariat for National Defence on two accounts energetically issued warnings to the Hungarian military authorities, reminding them of the consequences of such conduct, which was contrary to all international conventions and covenants. "From Hungary the answer was that it was a normal business transaction with which the Defence Ministry of our neighbouring country had nothing to do. "There are -- there is a total of 5.000 military officials in the 5th Army and musicians or whatever you, 9.000 and 18.000 soldiers throughout the territory of the 5th area of Slovenia, the whole of Croatia, part of Bosnia. We now have 80.000 armed with Kalashnikovs. And even if there were just 10.000 of them -- "Why did you go to Hungary, for heaven's sake? Didn't you have it at home? "Minister Spegelj considers that he knows the 5th military district very well. His shameful role of breaking up the units he was in command of until recently is contained in the statement 'We are at war with the army.' That was the statement made by the commander of the newly established chauvinistic detachments."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transcript, probably because of the speed at which the tape was being shown, a portion has been omitted. Spegelj said, and I think you could have heard this, when he says "We are at war," and he says "With whom?" and Spegelj answers "With the army, at war with the army." Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that time, they considered that they were at war with the army.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: At war with the Yugoslav People's Army, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell us, please, the showing of this footage, did it have an effect on the Croatian authorities admitting that they were in fact arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was even a deadline set by which the disarming should take place. So the Croatian authorities - I don't know exactly now, I didn't remember exactly - but the Croatian authorities asked that the deadline be extended by 20 days, the deadline previously established, but disarmament never took place. It was never carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you take a look at tab 73, now, please, and you will find a portion there -- yes, tab 73. It is part of Mesic's book, page 222 of the book. Do you have that portion, that excerpt?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I do have it in the tab, and I also have it in my notebook, which helped me with the quotations and the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Well, you can read it out, then. And it is page 222 from Mesic's book.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Before I go ahead with that, I'd just like to mention that Mr. Mesic wrote the book in 1994, that is to say, two years after these events had taken place, or three years later. And he first of all titled the book "How I Overthrew Yugoslavia." And then later on, he said that in talking with Mr. Hans Dietrich Genscher, having consulted him about the title of the book, Mr. Genscher, the then foreign minister of Germany, told him that a title like that would not be well-received in Europe. And then the working title of "How I Overthrew Yugoslavia" was changed by Mr. Mesic to read "How We Broke Up Yugoslavia," and that's what the first edition came out as, the heading. And then the title and heading was changed again and the book I'm quoting from is "How Yugoslavia Was Broken Up." Otherwise, you can see on page 222 of that book Mesic quite literally says the following: "That people, who were partially armed and partially armed youth were within the National Guards Corps and gradually organised into a modernly equipped Croatian army, they blocked the barracks --" Our word for that is kasavni [phoen] -- "and wherever possible they stopped movement of army troops." And there he means the units of the Yugoslav People's Army. And a little further on in the book, on page 276, for example, where he writes about the introduction of an embargo, an international embargo on weapons, imports to Yugoslavia, Mr. Mesic says the following: "We will now seize the weapons from Kadijevic's [inaudible]." That is on page 276. I must say that this seems almost impossible, that the president of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who has the post of the armed command, publicly states that Croatia's paramilitary forces would seize weapons from the Yugoslav People's Army for which he was its Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
