utterances.text: So we see that both Mesic and Spegelj are saying that they are in fact at war with the JNA. They didn't say at the time that they were at war with Serbia, did they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at the time, not yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now was Serbia ever at war with them or was it them who were at war with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, we have quite an obvious phenomenon of an armed uprising, an armed secession on the part of two federal units from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and waging war against the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, which pursuant to the constitution at that time until the 27th of April, 1992, was the sole legal, legitimate armed force in the country in Yugoslavia as an internationally recognised state and United Nations member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, let's take a look at two more short excerpts.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: May I be allowed to add the following, Mr. Milosevic: At the time, no mention is still made and it never entered anybody's minds to mention a war between Serbia and Croatia, and I myself as a member of the Presidency already and as vice-president of the Presidency toured the refugees in Borovo Selo, for example. I visited Bac Vajska. We had 8.000 refugees, mostly women and children, from Borovo Selo and the surrounding parts. And footage was made of that. I'm not sure we're going to have time to see that footage, but during my visit there I said -- and I was there not as a member of some sort of Serbian Bloc, Mr. Mesic and the authors of this indictment can -- constantly refer to the Serb bloc, which has no foundations in practice. If they wanted to call us anything, then they could have called us the protagonists of the federal option for the preservation of Yugoslavia, not as members of a Serb bloc. But anyway, during that visit of mine, for the media both domestic and foreign, I criticised the government of Ante Markovic and said they must deal with these refugees, see to them, see that they are cared for. This could not be left to Serbia alone to deal with, it must be brought to the care and attention of the entire federal government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We have two more short sections, short excerpts and footage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] If necessary, at a decisive moment, organise two or three men for the liquidation of the most dangerous ones. All right. Physical liquidation. You come to somebody's apartment, a messenger -- All right, I know. Appears at the door, dum, dum, dum, he goes downstairs. After that, let them look for the police and try to establish -- go downstairs, go to another one and yet another one or, rather at the same time. Those who are the most dangerous ones can be killed on their doorstep. It's not a question of women, children. Nothing, nothing, no questions asked. We are repeating the words of Spegelj and Boljkovac. If necessary, at a decisive moment, organise two or three men for the liquidation of the most dangerous ones. All right. Physical liquidation. You come to somebody's apartment, a messenger -- all right, I know. You appear at the door, dum, dum, dum, go downstairs. Afterwards, let them look for the police and let them establish. You walk downstairs, you go to another one and yet another one, or rather at the same time. Those who are the most dangerous ones can be killed on their doorstep. It doesn't matter. Women, children, nothing. Doesn't matter, no questions asked."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What does this footage show?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The army has nothing to seek there. It will be cut down. It is now a problem to protect you, the two of you, not from the army but from others. Oh, Fuck. Every officer is covered with five men. They will be cut down. I have to say that quickly now, who to separate, no doubt about that. No one should reach the barracks alive, no one. On the street, a soldier, anyone, a messenger. I don't know, when a signal is given, all of that should go down, no questions asked. "The minister of defence of Croatia believes that his system of organised killing of officers was fully elaborated. He orders the killing of soldiers and every member of the JNA in the street so that if an alert is sounded no one would reach barracks alive. "As for border posts, if there is disarming of border posts, all of them will be disarmed, as many as there are, but leaving Albanians five bullets each in their automatic rifles. As for the other ones, they should be locked up in basements and given food and water if this goes on for a few days. And as for this, if something happens, then just give instructions to all of your people who you know. Kill the extremists. On the spot, in the street, within the compounds of the barracks, anywhere else. Just a pistol and into the stomach. That will not be a war. It will be a civil war where there will be no mercy towards anyone, women, children. Into apartments. Quite simply, grenades thrown into family homes. "Repetition of what Martin Spegelj said. As for border posts, when border posts are disarmed, then they will be disarmed, all of them, as many as there are, but leave Albanians five bullets in their automatic rifles, and the rest locked up in cellars and given food and water if this goes on for a few days. As for this, if something happens, then just give instructions to all your people who you know. Kill extremists on the spot, in the street, in the compound, in barracks, anywhere. Just pistol and into the stomach. That will not be a war, it will be a civil war in which there is no mercy towards anyone, women or children. Into homes, family homes, quite simply grenades."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the question. The pace was very fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refreshed my memory of those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: What does this footage show, and the witness is obviously very upset, because he said that this jogged his memory, refreshed his memory.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: This looks so monstrous that when I watched this 14 years ago, Mr. Milosevic, quite simply I could not believe it. Really. At first I thought that this was editing, a montage, as intelligence services -- different intelligence services usually do, and I thought that was the case. However, later on this turned out not only to be original footage taken by the 12th department of the KOS, but everything that happened afterwards showed that this was original footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean "everything that happened afterwards"? Later on, did everything that Spegelj said here come true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps because there were these events and they happened quite some time ago, and for the Trial Chamber - and that is why we're here today - not much of this should really be enumerated. Everybody knows about the footage that went the world round when that member of the Yugoslav People's Army on an armoured vehicle in Split was almost strangled and a few soldiers killed in Trogir and Zadar, and Mr. Tudjman's call in Trogir and Zadar for the Croat industry to be reoriented to the manufacture of combat equipment and ammunition. A lot of that, really. Not to mention what happened later on when there were open attacks against the Yugoslav People's Army, and also fierce fighting with the units of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could another portion of the film be shown, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a technical problem? We're not seeing anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There shouldn't be a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] We are going to resolve Knin in that way, slaughter. We have international recognition for that, and then we slaughter them, especially now that this whore won in Serbia. "Milosevic? "Yes. Now, the Americans, the second day after he won, offered us all possible assistance on the very next day, and until then all were speculating they would or they wouldn't, now it's going to be this way, now it's going to be that way. Thousands of combat vehicles, this kind and that kind of cars, what do I know, for 100.000 soldiers complete arming free of charge. Repetition of what was said by Martin Spegelj. "We are going to resort to all resources. We're even going to use weapons. Knin we're going to resolve in the same way. We are going to slaughter everyone. We have international recognition for that that we're going to slaughter them now that this whore won in Serbia. "Milosevic? "Yes. Now the Americans, on the second day when he won, offered us all assistance, and until then everyone was speculating, they would, they wouldn't, this way, that way, 1.000 combat vehicles."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Note for Mr. Milosevic: The interpretation has not ended. We did not get transcripts that were translated. "[Voiceover] We are going to use all resources. We're going to weapons as well. Serbs in Croatia will never be there again for as long as we are there and we hope until now too their supremacy is a thing of the past. Their Knin will never be Knin again. We are going to enter Knin too. Knin has to disappear as Knin. All Croats should bear this in mind and we are going to create a state created at all costs, if necessary, at the cost of shedding blood. Repetition of the words of Josip Boljkovac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in this extract we've just watched, do we actually hear the voice of either of the ministers of the government of Croatia, or do we simply hear --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can hear the voice of one of the ministers and then the same is repeated by a presenter with better enunciation, because the voice is a bit -- well, distorted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did that apply in the case of both ministers, Spegelj first and then Boljkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every time, it would be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Knin, slaughter, expel. Was this an isolated position, a position held by Spegelj only? Boljkovac at the time was minister of the interior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this an individual position taken by Spegelj or was this a widespread position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, this was a very widespread view, taken not only in the top echelons of Croatian government but also beyond that, among the Croatian people. Because one must not lose sight of the fact that the political situation in Croatia today is quite different, in a favourable sense, compared to the time 14 or 15 years ago. And I have to say that the Croatian Democratic Union today, I really have to say that, is not the Croatian Democratic Union it was when it came to power during the first multi-party elections. At that time -- at that time, although hardly anybody believed us then, we kept warning that the Croatian Democratic Union has a Nazi, fascist, and chauvinist programme on the basis of how they treat the Serbs, their very own citizens on the territory where they live, where they had been living for several hundred years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the territory of Croatia. May I just say one more thing? This statement about the behaviour of the Americans also sounds convincing, because at least in my opinion, my opinion is today, as it was then, that although some authors dispute this, that the USA had a priority interest in preserving Yugoslavia and its territorial integrity as a whole but they wanted the political system changed throughout the territory and they wanted to keep their domination over that kind of entity. However, the interest of Germany was significantly different. Germany's primary interest was the secession of Croatia and Slovenia, and that proved to be correct later, and the United States of America could not do a thing about that. However, the United States, after that, showed their teeth in the case of Kosovo and they stationed their own troops there. In my assessment, in a way they were trying to separate Europe, and Germany in particular, from the near east and the Middle East, which is a region where America has special interests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what about the Serbs from Krajina? How did they feel about the expression of such views?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was in a position to read quite a bit about this. I was born in 1939, so I don't have personal memories of these terrible things that happened during the Second World War. It -- Montenegro was under Italian occupation but I read a great deal and in many contacts I was able to learn a great many things. When Mr. Hans Van den Broek first came to talk to me as vice-president of the Presidency, I tried to show to Mr. Hans Van den Broek a very small example of why the Serbs organised themselves and started an uprising in the Serb Krajinas in Croatia. This was a special issue of the Borba daily. Borba was a party newspaper of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and that was published ten years before all of this that happened. This special issue of Borba showed the complete list of 12.000 young boys and girls aged 6 to 12 only in the area of Podkozarje. If I'm not mistaken, that is close to the border of Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, in that entire list of 12.000 young boys and girls aged 6 to 12, during Pavlovic's Independent State of Croatia, all of them were liquidated, killed. It was not a list that was made just like that. It contained the names and surnames of all the children, the villages that they were from, and the names of both parents. When I showed Mr. Hans Van den Broek that list when we first met, he jumped from his chair and he said to me, "Well, Mr. Kostic, how long are you going to go on and on with this history of yours?" But believe me, 45 years is too short a period to forget such terrible crimes. Even in this election campaign in Croatia when Mr. Tudjman, as head of the HDZ, ran and won a landslide victory in these first elections, he stated that it is a historical lie and falsification that 700.000 Serbs, Gypsies, and Jews were killed in the Jasenovac camp. That was the largest concentration camp in the Second World War. Not only in the Balkans at that. Tudjman, as a general and as an historian, tried to reduce that number to a couple of tens of thousands. Then during the election campaign of his - and this was covered by the media - Tudjman visited his diaspora. It is a well-known fact that many Croatian emigres, after the Second World War, fled to the countries of the West, especially the USA, Canada, and South America. These people were war criminals, but they were forgiven. They remained unpunished because Croatia, after the Second World War, became part of the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia and practically it found itself on the side of the victorious allies. So it is a well-known fact that the Croatian authorities at that time opened the door wide for the return of all these Croatian emigres in the territory of Croatia. And even Mr. Martin Spegelj himself was -- well, how should I put this? -- in direct communication with these emigres. Now, look at this: When in many villages and towns of the Serb Krajina these Croatian policemen dressed in black uniforms with their symbols - and that is the chequerboard emblem which was also the symbol of -- the independent state of Croatia, Pavelic's state during the Second World War - when they appeared in those areas, of course they instilled fear. Fear was instilled as far back as the Second World War and there was a reawakening of that fear then, and then the people said en masse we are not going to allow a mass slaughter again like a herd of sheep, like what they did with us from 1941 to 1945. These people organised themselves, and this was truly self-organisation on the part of those people because the Croatian propaganda tried persistently to portray this as the result of infiltrated specialists, members of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, and so on and so forth. And I have to say, regrettably, that the authors of this indictment are either displaying a complete lack of understanding of all those events and deep misunderstandings of the -- deep misunderstanding of the roots and causes of that war in Croatia or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- Witness, please stop. Mr. Milosevic, the witness speaks, as one would expect, very clearly, but the procedure here is questions and short answers. Professor, short answers, not a long narrative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult to explain this briefly, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have to discipline yourself, Professor. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 26 of the Croatian indictment, it says: "Slobodan Milosevic, acting alone or in concert with other members of the joint criminal enterprise, participates in the joint criminal enterprise in the following way --" and then I will ask you only about subparagraph (m). "Controlled contributed to or otherwise utilised Serbian state-run media outlets to manipulate Serbian public opinion by spreading exaggerated and false messages of ethnically based attacks by Croats against Serb people in order to create an atmosphere of fear and hatred among Serbs living in Serbia and Croatia. The propaganda generated by the Serbian media was an important tool in contributing to the perpetration of crimes in Croatia." Now, please tell me, is it the case that the media spread exaggerated and false messages of ethnically based attacks against Serbs, and did I organise the media to spread such messages; and what do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I have to say that this atmosphere that prevailed in those days was very fevered. Ethnic and religious tensions had aggravated in the entire territory of Yugoslavia. I really cannot say whether you influenced the policies of those media and to what extent, but based on the conduct of some of the media in Montenegro that I know of, I can draw my own conclusions. For instance, when, after a session of the SFRY Presidency which elected Stjepan Mesic president of the Presidency of the SFRY, the Tanjug news agency gave a wrong news release to the effect that I voted for him as well. And one of the newspapers in Montenegro put me on a pillar of shame on its cover page, quoting that news, saying that I voted for a man who proclaimed already that he would be the last president of that state. I cannot say that anybody from the leadership of Montenegro commissioned that cover page. Maybe it was just the decision of the editorial board of that newspaper, but I can say two things: The conduct of the media in Serbia varied across the board. There was some media who preserved a moderate tone, trying not to aggravate tensions, but there were other media who deliberately planted misinformation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what they call state-run media outlets, were they moderate or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was coming to that. The state-run media in Serbia were more moderate than the rest, and what I was going to say when you interrupted me is this: It seems to me that at no other time, as far as I remember the history of politics in Yugoslavia, there had never been such a great number of electronic and other media available as in that time when these attacks happened. Even when we take into account the current time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I quoted to you from subparagraph (m), and it says: "False messages of ethnically based attacks against Serb people." Were there any ethnically based, ethnically motivated attacks against Serb people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Of course. Well, most of the attacks in that territory were ethnically based, because, you see --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my question. Is it the case that the Serbs, especially those living in Croatia, were subject to that atmosphere of fear?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Of course. That is indisputable. I wouldn't say really that it was an atmosphere of hatred from what I know from my contacts with them. It was an atmosphere of fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who created it and how?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The atmosphere of fear was created through all the developments that we've just discussed; through the media, through official appearances in electoral campaigns, at parliamentary elections. And if you add to that the practice that prevailed, you will understand. Throughout the post-war history, the Serbs in Croatia were a constituent people along with Croats. When the HDZ, headed by Tudjman, won power at multi-party elections, they simply threw them out of the constitution and the Serbs were reduced to the state of a minority, to the status of minority. And I had occasion to read many times writings about -- articles about the right to one's own language, et cetera. Serbs are not even mentioned there. They're treated as a minority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about that post-war period. The point was that they should forget about it all and then it all came back before their eyes. Let us see another piece of that -- another clip to hear what Simon Weisenthal said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I know, I know. You see, there is a book called "Mission, East-West," written by Herman Neuebacher, who was sent by Hitler to Croatia. After the war he was condemned in Yugoslavia to 20 years' imprisonment, and then he came back. He wrote a book about his interviews with Artukovic and others. They had told him, We have one problem with the Serbs: One-third of them must die, one-third must be converted to Catholicism, and one-third, may stay alive. That was their programme. "Such an irredenta on the part of all Ustashas and what remained of them. I used to see them everywhere; in Munich, in Paris. In their eyes, the war wasn't over. They did not feel defeated."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What Weisenthal was saying, was that the same thing could be observed in practice on the political arena in Croatia in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The very same thing. There's no need to stress that Mr. Weisenthal knew more about that than many others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lord Owen's book "The Balkan Odyssey" that is an exhibit here begins with the words, "Nothing is simple in the Balkans. Everything is permeated by history." So nothing is simple in the Balkans. Everything is permeated by history, and complexities introduce confusion into even the most careful study. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see another brief clip, depicting Lord Carrington.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "... war saw it differently. "The Serbs in Croatia and indeed outside Croatia. I have a very vivid memory of what happened in 1941, 1942, when Hitler declared Croatia as an independent puppet state, if you like, and the horrors that went on there and the murders of the Serbs are still very -- I mean, a very large number of Serbs were murdered at that time. I mean, hundreds of thousands. And I think it was very understandable that when Croatia declared its independence and promulgated a new constitution without any safeguard for the 600.000 Serbs who still lived in Croatia, that the Serbs were very perturbed about this."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with this appraisal of Lord Carrington's?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think it is clear from what I have said so far during this examination; it confirms what Mr. Carrington stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the new Croatian authorities' approach to the past, especially the Independent State of Croatia and Ustasha crimes in World War II?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: It is my impression that it would be extremely wrong and detrimental to treat the whole Croatian people as --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not mention the Croatian people. I talked about Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I did not pick up the wording of your question when I said this, but since I had to live with those problems, I know there were exaggerations in those days regarding those problems, and even aspirations to blame the whole Croatian people for the Ustasha movement. But as for Croatian authorities, I believe that to the very end they not only reasserted the Ustasha ideology from the Independent State of Croatia, which was a puppet state during World War II, they were proud of it and boasted of it. And all those who thought differently were suppressed. Their voice could not be heard. And all that was going on reminded me personally of something that I had occasion to hear in various films about the way Hitler acted towards Jews after the Nazis came to power in Germany, because in Croatia there were dismissals of Serbs, expulsions, destruction of their property. Let me just remind you of the events in Trogir town when Croatian citizens demonstrated against Serbs, which meant not only a physical danger to them but also destruction of their property.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see another video clip that could be commented upon in view of your explanation. It is a brief footage of the Lisinski hall at one of Tudjman's speeches.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] They see in the programmed objectives of the HDZ only demands to restore the Ustasha Independent State of Croatia. In doing so, they seem to forget that the Independent State of Croatia was not only a pure quisling creature and a fascist crime but it was also an expression of historic aspirations of the Croatian nation to have their independent state, and it is also a realisation of international factors, in the case of the government of Hitler's Germany, that on the ruins of the Versailles agreement tailored a new European order, those aspirations of Croatia and its geographic borders. "Unlike more discreet members of the ruling HDZ party, Glavas made no secret of his identification with the World War II Croatian Ustasha as he welcomed returning Croatian prisoners of war. "While some French ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you said an atmosphere of fear was created based not only on memories but also based on the facts of life at the time. You didn't, however, feel that there was an atmosphere of hatred on the part of Serbs against Croats. On what do you base that opinion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: In the course of that year that I spent on the Presidency of the SFRY, I had occasion to receive several delegations of Serbs from those Croat territories. At their request, I believe that I received two such delegations, and I think both of them were from Western Slavonia. I have to say that at that time, we did not have the capacity to create a buffer zone using units of the Yugoslav People's Army in Western Slavonia as we had done in Knin-Krajina, because in Knin-Krajina we had a very strong Knin Corps. In the Western Slavonia we were not able to do it for the simple reason that the troops of the Yugoslav People's Army were significantly reduced at the time because Croats, Slovenes, Macedonians, Kosovo Albanians, and others stopped sending soldiers to the army, and we had a big problem. And the troops that could have been used to protect those people in danger, Serbs in Croatia, were not available. So they came to see me, asking me to help somehow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Remember the procedure we are following.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the tape is running, and it would be better if it stopped. Secondly, there were two events depicted --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not ask for the tape to run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but you have to control it. There are two events depicted in the last clip that we saw. One was a speech, and the other was said to be returning prisoners of war. What were the dates of these events?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the dates are indicated on the tape itself. This speech of Tudjman in the Lisinski hall happened in the very beginning, when he said this Independent State of Croatia was not a pure quisling creature but a result of historic aspirations. He was practically justifying what Weisenthal clearly qualified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't need to know more explanation, just the date --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will check it out and tell you. I think the dates were written up on the footage itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I noted on the video it was written as 9th of September, 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then the date of the returning prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure. So that can be checked and be informed to us later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, in tab 1 you have the stenographic notes of a meeting you had with - how shall I put this? - a completely unbiased foreign politician. Now, I should like, from those notes, to quote some of your -- some of your positions, or maybe I'll ask you to do so, and then compare what you said at the time with what you think now to see whether it coincides and whether that was how it was. Now, to make things clearer for all the people attending these proceedings, what I have is this: Lisinski, the speech in the Lisinski hall on the 27th and 28th of February, and Glavas. That is the autumn of 1991, the autumn of 1991. When we reviewed these stenographic notes, you said that you had made a selection because we were dealing with a country which was very far away and completely uninvolved in the whole issue. It was a country in quite a different continent, in fact. And it was a friendly country at the same time, and you said everything you thought of at the time. You gave them your thoughts, and it was a conversation you in fact had with the foreign minister of the Republic of Zimbabwe in 1992. Take a look at page 2, please. What did you explain to the minister there? And I'm referring to paragraphs 2, 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the -- these are the original stenographic notes of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I understand it that it was the unauthorised version, the transcript of it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was what I said orally. I didn't have a written expose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: It says: "Croatian propaganda very successfully imposed upon the international public opinion that it -- that a small country, Croatia, was now allegedly being threatened by a large Serbia. And in that propaganda, they used all the elements which were acceptable to the ears of the international community. They tried to represent to the international community that that Yugoslav People's Army -" and in quotations - "'as a second force of the Soviet Union' in that part of Europe, was conducting aggression against 'that small country of Croatia.' They endeavoured to represent this as being a conflict between two ideologies, as if the alleged remnants of Bolshevism in Serbia and Montenegro were seeking, through the army, to settle accounts with the young regime in Croatia and Slovenia. A lot of effort was needed in the international community and with the international public to have the truth come out in public. I'm sure you know that Mr. Baker, only after several days, finally made a public statement and said --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Professor. I can see that on the screen we don't have the proper portion of the transcript, and it doesn't reflect what you're saying now, what Professor Kostic is talking about. The quotation he started with is the last paragraph in the English translation, which starts with "Croatian propaganda has been very successful ... [In English] ... international public opinion," et cetera. [Interpretation] Would you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "You are well aware of the fact that Mr. Baker finally stated in public that the cause of the crisis in Yugoslavia was unilateral secession by Slovenia and Croatia and their use of force."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us now, Professor Kostic, in connection with the explanation you have given us or, rather, the explanation you gave to friendly politician from a very far off country, from another continent altogether, whether, viewed from today's perspectives, that was indeed what happened.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, it is common knowledge that with Zimbabwe and a large number of other countries from Africa and Asia we were together with them in the non-aligned movement and had very close, friendly ties with those countries. Now, this meeting with the foreign minister of Zimbabwe was truly a meeting of friends, and we had very frank discussions, sincere discussions, and it was as if I had taken the solemn declaration then as I did here today in front of this Court, so I have nothing to add to the assessment and appraisal that I made there when I never knew that anything like that could happen or that this could be the subject discussed at an international tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You explained what happened because Baker did indeed say in public -- he said what the crisis was, and that was the unilateral secession of Slovenia and Croatia, and we have that on various tapes, we will be able to see that for ourselves, but tell me now, that conviction of yours that finally the truth came out, that it was a lengthy process.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No. It lasted a very short period of time because the United States of America were taken up with other problems, more major problems on a world level. So the problems of the Balkans were left to Europe to deal with. And Germany, in a very short space of time as a leading country in the European Community, managed very successfully to impose its own positions and views on all the other countries within the European Community. And in my own book, which is titled "1991, Let It Not Be Forgotten," which is also part of these tabs and binders, said that Europe during those days was not the Europe of DeGaulle or Churchill but that it was the Europe of Chamberlain and Paterna in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3 you go on to say, in paragraph 2, the last three lines, you say: "In a Croatia that totalitarian communist regime was replaced by another totalitarian regime founded upon pure national chauvinism." That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: And that's what I think today, too, for those times, although I've already said that the present situation in the Croatian democratic community on the political arena is far more positive compared to those times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on page 4 you inform your collocutor with Yugoslavia stands and positions. That is paragraph 2 or, rather, in the last paragraph, because it's a short page. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "At no point in time did we challenge the right of Slovenia and Croatia or any of the other republics to be able to secede from Yugoslavia, but we considered that that secession and stepping out from Yugoslavia should be done in conformity with the constitution and democratic procedure"? which they have not respected, which of course -- "Slovenia and Croatia as parts of Yugoslavia formed their own paramilitary formations in contravention of the constitution. At the very start, with its paramilitary formations, Slovenia seized control of the border crossings and all functions at the Yugoslav border in the area of Slovenia. That is to say the customs, the Ministry of the Interior, and so on. The Croatian authorities took power with a national chauvinistic programme on the idea of forming an independent Croatian state. In the previous constitution of the Republic of Croatia, Croatia consisted of two constituent peoples, the Serbs and the Croats. The Croatian authorities erased the Serbian people from the new constitution and decided to form a national State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he goes on to ask you, "Did Serbs have constitutional rights in that previous constitution?" And what was your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had absolutely the same rights as the Croats. Croatia was constituted as a republic of the Croatian and Serbian people because the Serbian people had been living in those parts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the document is before us, and we can read it. It doesn't seem to me that any useful purpose is served by taking the witness through it. I think you have sufficiently highlighted the important points.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With your permission, one more thing, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I commented on this with the witness, because at the time, he gave assessments and appraisals which he holds true today. He considers them to be valid today because they are truthful ones. That is the simple truth of it. And they cannot be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we're not going to deal with Tudjman, but on page 9 there is a very small paragraph, section. It is the second paragraph, in fact. And you say the Serbian people -- let me just find it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, give us the beginning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just see. It's a just a very short sentence. "The Serbian people in the area were frightened that they could suffer the same fate as they did in 1941." That's page 5, paragraph 4. The Serbian people in that area were afraid that they would suffer the same fate, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's what you explained to us a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you go on to explain on the following page, when it comes to the initiative and the Security Council, "When we sent an initiative to the Security Council," what does it say, for sending peace forces. That's on page 10, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Did you say page 10?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "When we sent an initiative to the Security Council to send peace forces, by that engagement on the part of peace forces, we expressed the readiness to withdraw the army from that area but the United Nations forces should protect the Serbian population because we reckoned that this would bring an end to a military conflicts and then we would seek a political solution to the status of that people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We won't dwell on that any longer, although this is a very - how shall I put this? - exact explanation, although a lengthy one, of the events that took place, and contemporaneous ones. But as most of it has been translated, we'll leave that for now so that everybody can read it for themselves if they're interested. But just to conclude. Apart from your assessments to the effect that the truth finally came out when Baker published what he published, everything else that it says here is in its entirety what you believe and think today, is that it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how did the SFRY Presidency react to all these events and especially the import of weapons, the fact that people were being supplied with weapons and so on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia before I came to join the Presidency held several meetings at which it sized up the situation and said that it was highly serious. It made rulings about the disarmament of paramilitaries which were not implemented, and when the situation came to a head and became even more tense, that's when we had the famous March session on the 12th or 13th or 14th and 15th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's leave March for the moment and let's have a look at tab 6 first, and we have there an order of the 9th of January, by the Presidency of the SFRY, which you mentioned. Let's me find it. It is the first document in the second binder. Have you had a chance of looking at that document before coming in to testify, looking at the order, or do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember this particular order from the time it was given, but I have had an opportunity of looking through it in the tabs and binders which contain practically all the decisions made by the SFRY Presidency in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mention is made here of secret import of weapons from neighbouring and other countries, for example, that they are being distributed to citizens according to their ethnic affiliation and political affiliation and orientation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it says, "Within the frameworks of political parties, illegal armed paramilitary units are being created. Through their existence and planned terrorist activities these pose a direct danger for the outbreak of armed insurrection and inter-ethnic conflicts on a very large scale with unforeseeable consequences." And then the Presidency issues its order. What is the essence and substance of the order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: In addition to what I said previously, it's important to note here that this is a united stand taken by the SFRY Presidency, and the president was Dr. Borislav Jovic and vice-president was Dr. Stipe Mesic. In the Presidency we also had Mr. Drnovsek -- yes, Mr. Drnovsek and also Mr. Tupurkovski. So it was the united assessment of the Presidency. There was Mr. Nenad Bucin as well, representing Montenegro in the Presidency, and as you can see in all the points, the individual points, from the first point dealing with disarmament then secondly paramilitary formations and then weapons and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clarify one point before we go into this. The order being issued is that on the territory of Yugoslavia all the armed compositions not within the frameworks of the SFRY should be disarmed, or organs of the interior whose organisation has not been established in keeping with federal regulations must be disbanded. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The second point deals with equipment and weapons of the armed units. Described under item 1 herein must be surrendered immediately to the nearest units of the JNA or institutions of the JNA, regardless of whether they have been collected by individual organs in the republics or are in the possession of various groups and individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you have anything to say about why this order issued by the Presidency - and you did mention all the members of the Presidency who took part in compiling and issuing the decision, from all the republics, might I add, that was an order that the Presidency adopted without any opposition or any dissenting views among its members - why then it was not put into practice?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, the answer is simple: Quite obviously, the members of the Presidency of the SFRY, who represented at that time Slovenia and Croatia as well, were close associates of the republican leaderships who had already opted for the war option. And Mr. Mesic throughout the time was the prime associate of President Tudjman and Mr. Drnovsek the first associate of Mr. Kucan who was president of Slovenia. And from many statements that they made and that you could hear bandied about and their public appearances as well -- Mr. Tudjman, for example, stated in public and this was later on taken up by Mr. Mesic -- much later confirmed by Mr. Mesic, in fact, that Croatia was only conscious of the fact that by going to war could it gain its independence. Mr. Tudjman said that himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think that? Do you think that position of his was right in view of what you said and what you quoted from the stenographic notes? And this was the well-known stance of the Yugoslav leadership of Serbia, Montenegro, and so on; namely, that no one was opposed to any kind of secession through a democratic, lawful, legitimate procedure.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, it was clear to them in Croatia that they could not free themselves of the Serb people on the territory of the Republic of Croatia without a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they didn't want a legal procedure because that way they'd have Serbs left in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, they'd have Serbs left in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that that is the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- I think it's going much too far. I'm very reluctant to interrupt and I didn't do it at many times before now, but that's really going too far. It's so leading. It's just actually putting words in the mouth of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Quite so, Mr. Milosevic. The questions are very, very leading. We are going to adjourn now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would the Court allow me just a couple of minutes, in the absence of this witness and nothing to do with his evidence, to deal with a couple of very short administrative matters? I shan't be here at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. You may leave now, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to this comment made by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, who says that I am putting words into the witness's mouth, I assume that she will not protest if she hears that from the mouth of the president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, and that she is not going to say that I put those same words into Tudjman's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's not the point. You're not to ask leading questions. You're not to give the evidence. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three very short things. First, I was very concerned about the way things developed with the witness's notebook this morning. I've reviewed the history and the transcript. I regret very much the way things developed, and of course accept responsibility for them. Although the history of the production and the lack of time yesterday, inability or whatever to ask questions about the notebook yesterday and the fact that it was handed back to him as he was walking out this morning all played their part, I can see that in my first observations this morning, where I was intending to express neutrality about the document and to say that by not cross-examining on it we were making no concessions, I went further or certainly could have been inferred or understood as going further than I should have done. That led to questions and again, although I attempted to preserve the neutrality position, it could be interpreted in another way, and I'm very sorry that that happened. My position remains the position that I acknowledged to His Honour Judge Bonomy. Second short point, very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that clarification, Mr. Nice, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. Second, the Court asked me yesterday about the grading of blue book assessments. I gather it's simply a standard NATO grading. It runs from A to F and 1 to 5. I don't think there's material available to us, and probably the Chamber wouldn't want it, as to how it is they -- they calculate within that grade. If you want it, we can find it, but it's A to F and 1 to 5, and it's a standard NATO grading. The last of the three matters, please, is something that we touched on earlier in private session. Although I'm basically going to adopt the position that was proposed in the private session, probably, with your leave, we should just touch on that in private session again, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, before I continue, I would like to ask you in respect of the stenographic notes contained in tab 1 that you said you had in translation, could you please admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there are parts of that -- of those notes which relate to Bosnia. Did you intend to lead any evidence relating to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this witness certainly has knowledge, and he took part in some political events that have to do with Bosnia and Herzegovina too. He headed the state Presidency until mid-1992, practically until the end of all the Croatian conflicts. So the highest relevance is for Croatia, but partly there is relevance as far as Bosnia is concerned as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you're going to lead evidence through this witness from these notes? I just wanted to make sure that you haven't overlooked it. It's a matter for you how you manage your case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will single out a few things in relation to this exhibit that have to do with Bosnia, but I will do that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit it. Give a number to the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the binder will be Exhibit D333.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, through the liaison officer I have just received some information that has to do with the evidence of a particular witness, but in view of the nature of its content, as you will see, I'm just going to ask for a private session for half a minute, because it has to do with the private affairs of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, we are not going to go back to the order of the Presidency dated the 9th of January. My next question has to do with the following: This illegally armed -- this illegal weapons that were imported, were they used eventually in the inter-ethnic conflict before the session of the Presidency on the 15th of May -- of March, referred to in paragraph 99 of the Croatian indictment and also in the Bosnian indictment, which is identical? I have to read this out to you. "In March 1991, the work of the collective Federal Presidency had been blocked due to a few questions among which was the issue of instituting a state of emergency in Yugoslavia." I'm not going to quote it further because it is not relevant for this question but it is relevant, and how, in terms of other questions, so I will restrict myself to this. So were these weapons used in the armed conflicts before the session in question?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: It was being used, especially in the territories inhabited by a majority Serb population in Croatia. We have just seen some footage, and that was a well-known fact in the public then. There were many incidents at that time in those areas, allegedly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mention any of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: There were several, but I think that most often Pakrac was referred to in terms of these incidents. Also at Lake Plitvice. I read the indictment carefully and the paragraph that has to do with that, and I think that it erroneously interprets everything that happened there. In that paragraph of the indictment, it says that there were conflicts there when the Croatian authorities tried to resume control over the area, which is a misrepresentation of the situation, because in all of these areas where there was a majority Serb population, there were police stations, and of course it is quite certain that these police stations were manned by persons from that territory, and they were Serbs, but they were part of the Croatian authorities in that way. However, this has to do with something completely different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is your answer to the question whether before that session of the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- there were incidents?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the position of the state and military leadership vis-a-vis these incidents? Can this be seen, for example? We have here in tab 57 what Admiral Brovet said on the 5th of March. Can you look that up, please, in your papers.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the 5th of March, 1991. That is ten days prior to this session of the Presidency. First of all, do you recall who Admiral Stane Brovet was and what he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Admiral Stane Brovet was a highly respected officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. He was an ethnic Slovene, and at that time he held the office of deputy federal secretary for national defence. The secretary was Veljko Kadijevic. And at the time he made a statement which pertains precisely to that. That's in tab 57.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's the one that I asked you to look up, to open.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is where he speaks about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the very beginning, he says that on the 2nd of March -- or, rather, he is speaking at a session of the National Defence Committee of the National Assembly of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As deputy minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the minister was absent. He says that: "At 600 hours on the 2nd of March, about 200 members of the Croatian MUP surrounded and stormed the Municipal Assembly and police station in Pakrac. Immediately prior to this, some of the active-duty and reserve forces from the police station left Pakrac with their weapons while between 15 and 20 reserve duty members, who remained in the station, were disarmed and detained by the forces that stormed Pakrac. As events unfolded, these forces increased without letup."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then he explains that citizens gathered there.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then they would disperse by force.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's when the Yugoslav People's Army was engaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also said here that during the previously mentioned events, fire was opened, that --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As soon as the Ministry of Defence was informed, they suggested to the Presidency that there be movement of appropriate units of the JNA, which the Presidency accepted, so they were engaged in Pakrac. And he says that this proceeds from the constitutional role of the JNA to, inter alia, prevent the outbreak of armed conflict, in particular inter-ethnic armed conflict, wherever such conflict is underway or about to break out. He also stresses that the Ministry of Defence has not entered into the causes and other circumstances that led to the conflict, particularly not into reasons of a political nature, because they believe the political problems should be resolved by political means and not by force.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: He says that people are fearful, that they feel this uncertainty, and they want this state of anarchy and lawlessness to be brought to an end to make it possible for the rule of law to prevail and to prevent civil war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also says that during the engagement of JNA forces in Pakrac the MUP of Croatia opened fire from an armoured vehicle at members of the JNA. He says that it's the fault of the MUP members for opening fire and that he asks for them to be held accountable.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Finally, when he made this report in the Federal Assembly, he said that the JNA has to fulfil its role in that situation, and that role is to ensure the safety of all citizens of Yugoslavia. And the JNA will stay in Pakrac until the situation normalises pursuant a decision of the SFRY Presidency from its session of the 2nd and 3rd March and until the situation is restored to what it was before the incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the session takes place and so on. Now, could you please comment on this quotation in paragraph 98 concerning these incidents. These events are described in their way: "In March 1991, the conflict intensified when Serb police forces attempted to consolidate power over areas with significant Serb populations. The Serb police, headed by Milan Martic, took control of a police station in Pakrac and battles erupted when the Croatian government attempted to re-establish its authority in the area." That is the same event. "At Plitvice, a bus carrying Croatian policemen was attacked by Serbs and another battle erupted. The JNA deployed troops in the area and issued an ultimatum for the Croatian police to withdraw from Plitvice." Are these allegations in paragraph 98 correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think it is a wrong interpretation, a matter of wrong interpretation in both paragraphs you quoted. The causes of both incidents lay in the attempt of the Croatian authorities to deal with the police that existed in those police stations, and who were Serbs, by replacing them with Croats. And as we said before, not only the existing police force in that area but also in the areas with majority Serb population, people did not allow those new units of Croatian policemen to take over those police stations for the simple reason that they were wearing those uniforms and the emblems that reminded those people of the atrocious genocide of World War II.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us disregard for the moment what they reminded them of. Let us just recall what Admiral Brovet, deputy minister of defence, an ethnic Slovene, who definitely cannot be a Serb nationalist, said that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we have a reference, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, where are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am reading from paragraph 57, which is the report of Admiral Brovet of the 5th of March, that is, three days later. He made a report to the appropriate committee of the federal parliament in charge of national defence of the event.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 57A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, it's the English translation that's 57A. 57 is the Serbian version. The letter A always denotes the English version. So in this 98 paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 57A, for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that's just one page -- two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: 5th of March, 1991, at 0600 from 2nd of March, about 200 members of the --" MUP -- it begins with these words -- have you found it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where in that document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: First paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's also on the ELMO in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it says here Brovet reporting to the competent committee of the federal parliament. He says that: "200 members of the Croatian MUP surrounded and stormed the Municipal Assembly and the police station," and stormed them. Then he describes the reaction of the citizenry and what happened next. And then in paragraph 98, it says "The conflict intensified when Serb police forces attempted consolidate power."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: This claim is absolutely nonsensical. Everywhere incidents occurred when Croatian authorities tried to commit some sort of questioned violence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, violence. So what is your answer? Are these allegations in the indictment that I quoted correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, they are not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us see a brief video clip from that session of the Presidency of the 15th of March. We've seen some of it before prematurely on the screens. I hope it can be played again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] And do you think you have the right to import arms illegally, contrary to the constitution and the legislation of Yugoslavia and to keep doing that and going on with the civil war? And don't you lecture me about God knows what. These are the answers to the questions, because those are the facts that you published. You decided to suspend federal laws on your territory. "Mesic: Serbia is more -- "Jovic: Please. All -- everything -- the same thing applies to everyone. Why don't you say a word about how you are breaking up the country. You are usurping other people's rights. That will not fly. "Mesic: Everybody is doing that. "Jovic: No use saying that. All those theories are not worth a dime. We are talking about very specific things, about people usurping other people's rights, and that will not be allowed. "Mesic: Boro, I just have one -- "Jovic: Please, there is not one thing that you can tell me. You are going into civil war with people who live in your territory and you are thereby causing a civil war in Yugoslavia. Those are facts that nobody can refute."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. It was even partially interpreted, and you were able to hear it in Serbian. Who are those two men that we can hear?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The one who spoke was Dr. Borisav Jovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were two of them.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: If we look at the screen, he is on the right. He was president of the Presidency of the SFRY at the time. And the man next to him is Mr. Stjepan Mesic. He was vice-president of the SFRY Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding this event, I have already quoted to you from paragraph 99. Do you think it's necessary for you to give further explanation about the disagreement between those who supported the initiative of the General Staff and those who opposed it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I need to stress it any further. The fact is that those who advocated the acceptance of that proposal by the General Staff thought that imposing a state of emergency and taking those measures could forestall further spreading of inter-ethnic conflicts and the accelerated movement towards civil war. Those who opposed it, who were representatives of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, and Macedonia, believed that imposing a state of emergency and giving more power to the military could cause a civil war in the country. At least, that is how they explained their refusal of the state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us look for a moment at something that could be very graphic, and that is a proposal that was to be accepted and published by the Presidency. Look at tab 58.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it's just one page. You have it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a draft release proposed by the General Staff of the Supreme Command to the Presidency that could not be accepted because four members of the Presidency resisted it; representatives of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is it. It's similar to the proposal of measures made on the 9th of January that were suggested to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were never implemented?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They were never implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now the Presidency is again trying to adopt the following. What is written here? The Presidency was supposed to adopt it, and it would have adopted it had there at least one more representative in favour.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "First, take measures to put the armed forces of the SFRY on the alert at a level which would, according to the assessment of the Supreme Command Staff, guarantee the prevention of inter-ethnic armed conflict and civil war and ensure the conditions for a peaceful and democratic denouement of the Yugoslav crisis, based on the constitution and laws. "Second, take urgent and decisive measures with a view to bringing the country's disrupted defence system into the framework established by the SFRY constitution. For this purpose, the Order of the SFRY Presidency of the 9th of January, 1991, to disarm and disband illegal armed units, and the positions and decisions of the Presidency on control of the Territorial Defence and performance of conscription duties will be consistently implemented."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "In adopting this decision, the SFRY Presidency indicated the need to intensify constructive and democratic dialogue on overcoming the economic, political and constitutional crisis and on the future organisation of Yugoslavia. "The SFRY Presidency once more --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Emphasises, and so on. And it says "shall use the means prescribed by the --" et cetera. It will say -- "It will oppose the legally prescribed measures to all forms of anarchy, lawlessness, the adoption of unilateral decisions, and the policy of fait accompli."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that did not go through at that session of the Presidency. They were unable to adopt it. Let me now go back to the paragraph 56 that was quoted. I already quoted the first three lines, but I have to do so again. "The work of the Presidency reached a deadlock on several issues, including the imposition of the state of emergency." We have just seen what was proposed. And then it goes on to say: "Members of the Presidency from Serbia, Montenegro, province of Vojvodina and province of Kosovo resigned from their positions. In his speech of the 16th of March, 1991, broadcast by the television, Slobodan Milosevic, as president of the Republic of Serbia, stated that Yugoslavia is finished and that Serbia is no longer bound by the decisions of the Federal Presidency." Now, let us see if this is true and accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that was paragraph 99 of the Croatian indictment, not --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 99 of the Croatian indictment, but it is identical to paragraph 56 of the Kosovo indictment -- or, rather, the Bosnian indictment. It refers to my speech. I'm sorry, because I have that speech as published in Politika newspaper of the 17th of March, but unfortunately I didn't note it down correctly. It's tab, I believe, 51. Let me look for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 51.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's 51. I hope it's translated, although I haven't read the translation. Just a minute. I did not check the English translation, but let us stop for a moment here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the Politika newspaper, the front page, and here in paragraphs 99 and 56 that are identical, it says: "In his speech, on -- in his speech in March, Slobodan Milosevic stated that Yugoslavia is finished." Now, please look -- please read, in fact, from the beginning of my speech, because a claim is made that I stated in that speech that Yugoslavia is finished. What did I actually say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "Last night, Yugoslavia entered the final phase of its agony. The Presidency of the SFRY has not been functioning for a long time now, and any illusions about its efforts and endeavours which are in fact non-existent are now definitely dead."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is dead, Yugoslavia or what?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The illusions that the Presidency is functioning are dead, and the allegations in the indictment are completely wrongly interpreting this text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since it says, nevertheless, that I stated that Yugoslavia is dead, would you read on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "This is --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do not have the exact reference where it is exactly in the speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So from this entire passage in the indictment, what is only partially true is the part at the end from which we can see that in that speech, far from claiming that Yugoslavia is dead, you remained dedicated to the idea of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But tell me, is there any truth in this allegation? Let us look at paragraphs 99 and 56. Are they correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Only a small bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I mean the bit where it says that I said Yugoslavia was dead?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No. You said in your speech that it is an illusion that the Presidency is trying to resolve it. That illusion was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It was an illusion that they were doing something when they were doing nothing. Now, there is another allegation. It says that members of the Presidency of Serbia, Montenegro, and the province of Kosovo and the province of Vojvodina all resigned from their posts. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty about all of them, but I know for a fact that Borisav Jovic resigned as president of the Presidency of the SFRY, and the member for Montenegro, Nenad Bucin. In the release of Tanjug news agency, they wrote that Jugoslav Kostic also announced his resignation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Riza Sapundzija ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think he was actually replaced at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In your opinion, since you explained why those who resigned did so -- did you explain?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I really had no opportunity to talk to any one of them about that, but what they stated publicly was that they did not wish to participate in the breaking up of Yugoslavia or to bear responsibility for that because they thought that such decisions of the staff of the Supreme Command were leading Yugoslavia straight into civil war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in your opinion, in your assessment, because after that you went on to be vice-president of the Presidency, did this failure of the Presidency to adopt this proposal of the staff of the Supreme Command mean a failure of the Presidency to fulfil its role and obligations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think this was a failure of the Presidency to fulfil its constitutional obligation, because that obligation was to preserve peace and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. And I think this was a grave violation of that obligation. Several times I said publicly, and I wrote in my book, that in my assessment the adoption of that proposal of the staff of the Supreme Command at the session of the 12th, 13th, and 14th of March was perhaps the last chance to prevent a broad civil war, wide-scale civil war in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 58, it says: "Take measures to raise the alertness and readiness of the armed forces with a view to preventing civil war and inter-ethnic armed conflict." That was not accepted.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
