utterances.text: And how did the staff of the Supreme Command react --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you proceed any further, so that I understand the way in which this worked. This was a Supreme Command of eight representatives which operated according to simple majority voting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me how -- in a democratic set-up like that, can you tell me how it helps to try to advance the debate to walk out just because your particular proposal does not get a majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there are a number of questions within the overall question that you put to me. First of all, the Presidency numbered eight members, and for any decision to go through, they needed at least five Presidency members to vote in favour of it for any decision to be taken. Now, as to the more important questions, the rules of procedure governing the work of the Presidency, a two-third majority was required, which means six members of the Presidency to vote in favour. And to all intents and purposes here, at this first session we were faced with a situation where four Presidency members voted in favour and four voted against. And then that meeting was interrupted, if I remember correctly, and on the following day, or two days later, it was continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you not able to answer -- are you not able to answer the question I asked you? I'd rather you did that than give me another reiteration of what I already know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do apologise, Mr. Bonomy, but then it would seem that I didn't understand your question. Would you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question was in a system like this which operates democratically according to the votes of the individual parties who come together to meet and form the Supreme Command, how does it help to advance the debate about the future of Yugoslavia just to walk away, to resign when you don't get your own way because your particular proposal is not accepted by a majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you understood the situation wrongly. Nobody walked away. All members of the Presidency stayed on throughout the duration of the meeting, and the meeting went on for three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've just told us that, as far as you can recollect, at least two members resigned thereafter, and Mr. Milosevic has put it to you that actually four resigned. So either way, people who were unhappy with the decision said, "I'm taking my football, I'm not playing any more, I'm walking away." Now, how does that advance sensible political debate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you're asking me what I personally think about those resignations which were tendered by them at the time, then I have to say this: In a situation of that kind, if we assess the situation in the country as being extremely critical, that without taking these measures this would lead directly to a civil war, then I think that had I been in their stead, in their place, for the same reasons and motives as put forward by them, that is to say that they no longer took -- wanted to take part in the country's disintegration, then I would have acted in the same way, the difference being that Dr. Jovic, several days later, pursuant to instructions from the Assembly of Serbia, went back to the work in the Presidency whereas Nenad Bucin remained by his decision to resign and didn't go back. So I'm differentiating between that. I don't know if that answers your question. I differentiate between voting at the session itself and the inability to make a decision from an act to resign from a body after the completion of a meeting and then that no steps were taken, because the resignations followed after the meeting had been completed on the third day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, if you abandon the democratic process, you must -- for a very strong reason, because you think that the decision made is fundamentally wrong, it's going to lead to the break-up of the state, if you abandon the democratic process in that situation and resign, you must have an alternative in mind, surely, to advance the interests of the state, and I'm trying to identify what it was thought by those resigning they could achieve by doing so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but I can't answer that question of yours. I don't know what they thought. All I was saying -- and I didn't have a chance to contact them, but I was only saying that if it was a very difficult situation that faced the country which was leading directly to a civil war, and the meeting lasted for three days, then you had eight members of the Presidency -- that's why I brought that up. Had there been at least nine of them, then you could have had a majority, and I would have respected the will of the majority. But there was a checkmate position, a stalemate, in actual fact, and had I been in the position of those people faced with such a grave responsibility as a member of the Presidency and Supreme Command, I might have reacted in the same way and tendered my resignation in the desire to make us more serious and reasonable in our actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to prolong this unnecessarily, but I wonder if it's correct to describe it as checkmate, because what you need is a positive vote to change things. And if you have an equality of voting, then you have the status quo. That wins the day. And one would expect in a democratic set-up that that would be recognised in spite of the strong views of everyone, whereas to walk away leaves a vacuum and indeed might well have precipitated the break-up of -- of the state. However, Mr. Milosevic will no doubt take up his own line of examination from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, might I be allowed to say this: I just have a fourth category, but I don't think that the mate and checkmate position are the same positions in chess, when either side, based on their views, have the chance to fight. And pursuant to constitutional solutions and decisions, it doesn't mean leaving a vacuum mind, not only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clarify the area broached by Mr. Bonomy. I think that he broached it very correctly. That's my personal opinion. But let's clarify matters at this point. Is it the most important constitutional obligation of Presidency members to prevent a war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to the constitution. An agreement was signed to that effect in the Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's leave that aside for the time being. I think we'll arrive at an understanding and explanation if we differentiate between the personal and institutional character and factor. So in the personal sense, Borisav Jovic is a person, and Nenad Bucin, to take just those from Serbia and Montenegro, tendered their resignations. Now, let's differentiate between the personal and institutional factor by way of your example, that is to say the example of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any vacuum that set in? You explained that they had tendered their resignations after the meeting. So they didn't leave before the meeting was over, but they personally considered it to be a personal act of responsibility on their part. Now, what happened? Bucin resigned and left it there. What happened afterwards? Montenegro reacted straight away and elected you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you appointed or elected?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Montenegro didn't elect me straight away, but pursuant to the constitution, it is regulated that in the case of, for example, Montenegro not having a representative in the SFRY Presidency, which happened when Mr. Nenad Bucin resigned, then according to the constitution, it was provided for that the president of the Presidency of the republic perform the function of the Presidency member, and that function was taken over until I was elected and chosen and confirmed in the Assembly by Mr. Momir Bulatovic, who at the time was the president of the Presidency of Montenegro, and that was the constitutional solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So there was no vacuum?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's why I said there was no vacuum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bucin resigned, Montenegro chose you. While you were -- actually took up your job, the president performed the function pursuant to the constitutional stipulations. Is that the substance of the matter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Jovic, at the request of the Assembly, withdrew his resignation and continued working in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we can move on. I'm sorry, but I have to take a moment to find something that I don't seem to be finding now. Let's look at the reactions of the staff of the Supreme Command to the non-adoption of its proposal, and you'll find that in tab 59 where we have an official statement by the Supreme Command staff of the armed forces of the SFRY, and it is dated the 19th of March, 1991. And that is tab 59.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you have it, Mr. Robinson, in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is what it talks about. It says that: "At its sessions held on the 12th, 14th, and 15th, the Presidency did not accept the proposal of the Supreme Command Staff to take appropriate measures guaranteeing the prevention of inter-ethnic armed conflict and civil war and ensure conditions for a peaceful and democratic resolution of the Yugoslav crisis based on the SFRY constitution and laws." And then it goes on to say: "The Supreme Command Staff, as the highest of expert professional body in command and control of the armed forces, made a comprehensive evaluation of the newly arisen situation and its possible consequences and states as follows. "That the JNA will steadfastly guard the SFRY borders, that it will not allow them -- that it will not allow international conflict -- inter-ethnic armed conflict and the use of force."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Or violent demonstrations, from whatever side, aimed at toppling the regime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it goes on to say that: "In view of the fact that the circumstances were not ripe for the 9th of January decision to go ahead, the Yugoslav People's Army cannot bear any responsibility for the possible continuation of illegal arming of citizens or their organising in military fashion anywhere on Yugoslav territory." And it reiterates that: "The conditions and measures are the key prerequisites for a peaceful and democratic solution of the Yugoslav crisis ..." So what do we have here? Who is it who is against the measures designed to prevent armed conflict on an ethnic basis?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think the greatest resistance was offered by representatives of the secessionist republics who later on broke away violently, seceded violently from Yugoslavia, as we saw later on. And I think that it is on -- on the basis of the information I had at the time and that went public at the time, it seems to me that the representatives in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the representatives of Macedonia as well joined in, joined them out of fear that something was not ascribed to them, that Slovenia and Croatia were not ascribing bias to them on their part, but they voted against the proposal by the staff of the Supreme Command as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you think -- do you think it's appropriate for an army to issue this sort of statement expressing dissatisfaction with a decision made by the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, all I can tell you is this: I can just tell you what I would have done in that same situation, but that doesn't mean that that was a good thing or that that would have been a good step, the right step. In my public statements and later on as the vice-president of the SFRY Presidency and a member of the Presidency, of course, on many occasions repeated what I said, that is to say that I consider and still consider today that it was the 11th hour for something to be done, to prevent the chaos of a civil war from breaking out on the territory. Had I been in that situation, I would have taken steps and introduced a state of emergency, but perhaps that might have been the wrong decision. It's difficult for me to say. And as far as Mr. Kadijevic is concerned, I said about him personally, when there were many criticisms made of him and many complaints about Mr. Kadijevic as the federal minister, at the time I myself said that in my opinion Mr. Kadijevic was more a politician than he was a soldier. And at no point did I allow in any sense any doubt to be thrown on and suspicions on Mr. Kadijevic, because in my opinion he always was and remains a Yugoslav according to his orientations and options.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you seem to be saying is that this is acceptable, for an army to make a statement like this which expresses dissatisfaction with a decision of its own Supreme Command. Now, if you had been one of those who was against a state of emergency, would you not have regarded such a statement as an act of disloyalty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. This kind of statement precisely speaks of loyalty of the army and the Supreme Command staff to the Supreme Command, the civilian leadership of the army. But that's why I said that perhaps had I been in the place of General Kadijevic, instead of this statement I might have taken steps, but I don't know whether it would have been the right steps to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you think the fifth paragraph, abandoning responsibility, is an acceptable way of stating the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, read out paragraph 5 before you answer and see what it's about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "Since the necessary conditions have not been met and prerequisites for the complete implementation of the order of the SFRY of the 9th of January, 1991, the Yugoslav People's Army cannot bear any responsibility for the possible continuation of illegal arming of citizens or their organising in military fashion anywhere on Yugoslav territory." Therefore, with this kind of statement, as I read it and understand it, the Supreme Command staff, respecting fully the check position or impasse that the Presidency faced with four votes for and four votes against, the Yugoslav People's Army, or the Supreme Command staff is stating that that situation which is already difficult and will continue to deteriorate in future. And that is why I'm not saying what my conduct would be had I been one of those eight members of the Presidency. What I tried to do was to explain, although that could be dangerous for me. Had I been in the place of the Defence Minister faced with an impasse of that kind and fully conscious of the difficulty of the situation, I might have taken steps on that day, bearing in mind that in a country of democracy, such as Greece, for example, the army did take steps in critical moments, and for practically seven years the country was governed by a military junta. But there was no civil war in Greece and democracy returned to Greece in a peaceful way later on. So I don't know whether this solution on my part would have been a good one, but that is what I would have done myself most probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll break for -- for today. There is another trial here at 2.15. So we will have to break now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, but might I just be allowed to ask one more question to clarify what Mr. Bonomy just raised. Might I be allowed to do that, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 says: "Since the SFRY Presidency adopts and accepts the proposed essential measures for the full implementation of its own order of the 9th of January 1991 --" It might be a good idea to read out the order prior to that. It is the Presidency's order to disarm and disband illegal armed units. So as this decision was not accepted, they go on to say that they won't be able to bear any responsibility for the situation. Had they done so by passing the order, they would have been acting unlawfully, and that's why they say whether -- now, whether that is correct or not, that is what they say, because the order was rejected. Was that a fact?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the fact precisely, and that's why I said that faced with a situation of that kind, and if I were in the minister's shoes, I might have acted differently even if it might have appeared to be illegal and unlawful, but faced with such grave decisions and the threat of a civil war, facing an impasse when civil authorities cannot take the right solution, I might have taken different steps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, Mr. Robinson that we have to adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn and resume on Wednesday, 1st February, at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
